pl-l4d41c2-d1e115.summary: Reports that others seem to allow marriage between in-laws in the fifth generation, and not to separate it if contracted in the fourth.

pl-l4d41c2-d1e118.summary: Cites Pope Fabian: relatives by affinity through husband or wife may marry in the fifth generation after the spouse's death; if joined in the fourth, they are not separated; in the third it is not lawful; a man is joined equally to his own and his wife's kin. Lombard notes this allows marriage in the fifth or fourth degree of affinity.
claims: Fabian permits affinity marriages in the fourth or fifth degree.

pl-l4d41c2-d1e124.summary: Cites Julius: no one may marry the widow of his wife's father, brother, or son, nor the widow of his wife's kin to the third generation; in the fourth and fifth, if found, they are not separated.

pl-l4d41c2-d1e131.summary: Notes how variously the authors speak: some require affinity to be observed to the seventh degree, others do not divide marriages in the fifth or fourth; the former state the rigor of truth, the latter the dispensation of mercy, since the Church can dispense in the union of in-laws beyond the third degree, as Gregory dispensed in the fourth degree of consanguinity.
claims: Rigor and dispensation explain the differing rules.
The Church can dispense in affinity beyond the third degree.

pl-l4d41c2-d1e137.summary: Cites Gregory to Bishop Venerius: whether a woman married to an outsider belongs to his kin, whether this remains after his death, whether it dissolves under another husband, and whether children of the later union can marry into the first husband's kin. If they were one flesh, how can kin belong to one and not the other? Affinity is not destroyed in the survivor by the other's death, nor dissolved by another marriage, nor may the children of another union join the first husband's kin; whoever thinks otherwise denies God's word that they shall be two in one flesh.
claims: Affinity survives the spouse's death and remarriage.
Children of a second marriage may not marry the first husband's kin.

pl-l4d41c2-d1e152.summary: Explains that this forbids children born of the second husband to marry the first husband's kin, since through their mother they belong to the kin of the first husband, with whom she was one flesh.
claims: Children of a second marriage share affinity through their mother.

pl-l4d41c2-d1e158.summary: Adds Innocent: a woman who passes to a second marriage and bears children cannot bring them into the first husband's kin; this is observed to the seventh degree, but especially to the third or fourth.
claims: The rule binds especially to the third or fourth degree.

pl-l4d41c2.summary: Others seem to allow marriage between in-laws in the fifth degree and not to separate those married in the fourth, as Fabian and Julius say. Lombard explains that the first authorities state the rigor of truth, the latter the dispensation of mercy, since the Church can dispense in affinity beyond the third degree, as Gregory dispensed in the fourth degree of consanguinity. Gregory to Venerius: affinity is not dissolved by a spouse's death or remarriage, and children of a second marriage cannot marry the first husband's kin; Innocent agrees, to be observed especially to the third or fourth degree.
claims: Some authorities permit marriage of in-laws in the fourth or fifth degree.
The seventh-degree rule is rigor; the others are dispensation.
The Church can dispense beyond the third degree of affinity.
Affinity survives a spouse's death and extends to children of a second marriage.
